before: A test compares an actual result with a stated expectation. Keep expected values independent of the implementation so the same mistake is not copied into both.

Arrange an input, call the method, then assert the expected result. This console example uses AssertEqual to throw an exception on a mismatch, stopping this run as a failure; it is not an MSTest or xUnit test project.

Math.Max returns the larger of its two arguments, keeping the discounted amount at least zero. The examples check a normal case, exactly the discount, and below it. Passing these checks is evidence for these cases, not proof for all inputs.
Expected behavior from this example: 3 checks passed. This expected result is a reasoned prediction until a compiler test is recorded.

Optional local transfer: Add tests for zero and another positive input. Then move the function into a real test project without claiming the quiz itself ran those tests. This is a separate local practice task, not a requirement to mark the reading complete.
after: An assertion is a check that must be true. AssertEqual compares the answer we expect with the answer the function actually returns.

The discount rule subtracts three but never goes below zero. Math.Max chooses the larger of zero and amount - 3. Expected test answers should come from that rule, not repeat the function's calculation.
These checks cover an ordinary amount, exactly three, and less than three. Each checks a different part of the rule.
The program prints 3 checks passed. Each actual answer matches its stated expectation, so no assertion throws.

A mismatch throws an exception and stops this small console run. Passing proves these three cases worked; it does not prove every possible input works. Larger projects use a test runner to collect and report many checks.
